paragraphs: The golden ratio is a special number that appears in many places, like nature, art, and buildings. It comes from a number sequence introduced to Europe by Leonardo Fibonacci in 1202, though it was discovered earlier by the Hindu scholar Pingala.

This sequence leads to a ratio that creates the “golden rectangle,” a shape that some people believe looks perfect. In the 1860s, Gustav Fechner claimed people preferred this shape, which helped create the idea that the golden ratio represents beauty. However, his study was later disproved. More recent experiments show that most people can’t even recognize the golden rectangle by sight. The golden ratio appears in sunflower spirals and other natural patterns, but nature doesn’t always follow it. Shells, for example, grow based on calcium levels, not math.

Some think human faces that match the golden ratio are more beautiful; however, this idea is not supported by science. It can create false beauty standards and misuse real mathematics. The golden ratio is interesting in art and nature, but it is not a rule for beauty. It is only one way to look at the world. Everyone’s view of beauty is different.

paragraphs: The golden ratio is a number that comes from a group of numbers called the Fibonacci sequence.

These numbers were used in Europe in 1202, and they create a shape called the golden rectangle. Some people think this shape looks very nice. Gustav Fechner said people liked it best, but later, others showed that he was not right. The golden ratio is in some flowers and other things in nature, but it is not in everything. For example, snail shells don’t grow with this number.

Some people use the golden ratio to say who is beautiful. They use it in apps or pictures on social media. But this is not true. Scientists say the golden ratio cannot show who is or is not beautiful. Everyone is different, and that is okay.
